intent: Write code that a competent stranger can read correctly without reconstructing hidden state, using the host language's own conventions rather than a private dialect.
problem: Code that needs the author to explain it — cryptic names, magic numbers, dense boolean expressions, bespoke control-flow idioms, commented-out remnants — makes every change a re-derivation, and reviewers approve changes they cannot fully verify.
context: Applies to every line, but pays off most in code that is read far more often than written. Readability here is not aesthetics: it is the property that lets a reviewer detect a defect, lets an on-call engineer locate the failure, and lets a new maintainer change the right thing. 'Idiomatic' matters as much as 'readable' because a reader's priors are the language's conventions, not your private style.
benefits: Reviewers can spot a semantic change instead of re-deriving the code.
On-call diagnosis starts from the name of the thing that broke, not from a search.
Onboarding time falls; the code explains itself.
Defects cluster in unreadable code, so readability improves where the bugs are.
Refactoring is possible at all — you cannot safely change what you cannot read.
tradeoffs: Long, intention-revealing names cost bytes and, in some languages, hurt (the binary is not the cost; the reader is).
Readability and raw brevity conflict constantly; the longer form is usually the readable one.
Strict idioms make code written by a non-native of the language look non-conforming to reviewers from another culture.
Naming is a skill with no compiler check; the principle cannot be enforced by a tool.
Heavy commenting and naming can obscure rather than clarify if the names merely restate the code.
quality_attributes_note: discoverability 9 and maintainability 9 are the point; extensibility 5 because readability is not an extension mechanism.

participants.responsibility: The competent stranger who must understand and change the code; the optimisation target.
participants.notes: Includes the author six months later and the on-call engineer at 03:00.

participants.responsibility: Carries the intent so the code needs no translation step.
participants.notes: If a name needs a comment, the name is wrong.

participants.responsibility: The language community's standard idiom, which supplies the reader's priors.
participants.notes: Deviating from convention is a cost paid by every future reader.

use_cases: Renaming `d` to `elapsedTimeInDays` so the comment can be deleted.
Replacing a four-term boolean expression with a named predicate function.
Naming a magic constant `passingScore` instead of 80.
Splitting a 90-line function whose control flow no longer fits on one screen.
Rewriting a clever one-liner in the language's ordinary form when the cleverness buys nothing.
avoid_when: A generated file whose source of truth is the generator template.
Code whose performance depends on a form the readable version cannot express (benchmarked, documented).
Domain code where the domain expert's term is opaque to programmers — use the domain term, do not translate it.
A language with strong compiler-enforced structure where the readability contribution is marginal.
pitfalls: Names that lie: `getList()` returning an array, or `count` that does not count.
Comments restating the code ("increment i by 1") instead of explaining why.
Noise words: Data, Info, Manager, Handler, Util prepended to everything.
Abbreviation in names that hides which of several similar things is meant.
Treating compressed cleverness as sophisticated when a reader needs to hold more state to parse it.

related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: The design-level sibling of this pattern: an interface named for what it does rather than what it contains.
related_patterns_notes.guard-clause: Invert the deeply nested `if` and the happy path stops being something the reader must reconstruct.
related_patterns_notes.make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Readable code is largely code that does not need to represent impossible states at all.

anti_patterns: Boolean parameters (`includeInactive=false`) that force the reader to evaluate a call site mentally.
Nested ternaries and dense boolean chains.
A private dialect: custom macros, bespoke null sentinels, or a house style that contradicts the language.
Functions whose name cannot be completed without a conjunction.
design_principles: Code is read far more often than it is written, so clarity for the reader is the governing constraint.
Names are everywhere in software; because we do so much of it, we'd better do it well (Clean Code, ch. 2).
If a name requires a comment to explain it, the name does not reveal its intent.
A name must be an honest reflection of the entity: disinformation (calling a Set a List) forces the reader to check the declaration.
Comment the why, not the what.
Follow the conventions of the language and its community before the conventions of the team.
best_practices: Rename on discovery; a better name found during review is applied immediately, not deferred.
Extract a named predicate or helper for any condition a reader would have to hold in their head.
Replace magic numbers with named constants at the point of first use, not in a central registry.
Keep comments for the reason a decision was made; delete the ones the code already states.
Run the formatter the language community uses, so layout stops carrying information.
Read the diff as a stranger before merging: if the change is not obvious from the diff, the names are wrong.
sources: Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Prentice Hall 2008 (ch. 2 Meaningful Names, ch. 3 Functions) — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/clean-code-a/9780136083238/toc.xhtml
Robert C. Martin, The Single Responsibility Principle, Clean Coder blog 2014 — https://blog.cleencoder.com/uncle-bob/2014/05/08/SingleReponsibilityPrinciple.html
Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd ed. — https://martinfowler.com/books/refactoring.html
